title: WHAT WOULD SELLING THIS SERVICE LOOK LIKE?
content:
Knowing what service you could perform is only part of the decision. The same skill can become very different businesses depending on how you package and deliver it.

A service can be a one-time project or something customers need continuously. It can be completely custom or standardized into a repeatable package. It can require you to be physically present or be delivered remotely. It can serve one customer at a time or several together.

These choices can mix. A remote service can still be custom. A local service can still be recurring. A group service can still have a standardized package.

DRAFT QUESTIONS
Would customers need this once or repeatedly?
How much of the work changes for every customer?
Do I need to be physically present?
Could multiple customers receive the service at once?
Most importantly: how much additional time does each additional customer require?

When you have a likely shape → PDF 43.
If the underlying service idea still feels wrong → PDF 40 or 41.

ONE-OFF OR ONGOING
Some services naturally end after a project. Others solve a problem that keeps returning.

CUSTOM OR STANDARDIZED
Custom work changes around each client. Standardized or productized service defines a more repeatable scope and process.

LOCAL OR REMOTE
Physical presence changes travel, equipment, service area, and scheduling. Remote delivery changes the possible customer base and tools.

INDIVIDUAL OR GROUP
Serving several customers together can reduce time per customer but changes the experience.

These dimensions combine. The purpose is to see the operational shape of the service, not force it into one label.

DIMENSION 1 - ONE-OFF / PROJECT VS ONGOING
Example: one website cleanup versus monthly maintenance.

DIMENSION 2 - CUSTOM VS STANDARDIZED / PRODUCTIZED
Every engagement built individually versus a defined package/process.

DIMENSION 3 - LOCAL VS REMOTE
Requires physical presence versus delivered online/phone/etc.

DIMENSION 4 - INDIVIDUAL VS GROUP
One customer/client at a time versus multiple customers receiving the service together.

COMBINATION EXAMPLES
Monthly remote bookkeeping -> ongoing + relatively standardized + remote + individual client.
Wedding photography -> one-off/project + partly custom + local + individual client.
Group fitness class -> ongoing or session-based + standardized + local/remote + group.
Custom website build -> project + custom + remote + individual client.

The dimensions help you see what operating the service might feel like before you commit to the offer.

THE SHAPE CAN CHANGE LATER
Your first version does not lock the service forever. A custom service can become more standardized after you learn which requests repeat. A local service can add remote components. An individual service can eventually add group delivery.

Choose the shape that makes sense for the service you can actually deliver now. Optimization can come after reality gives you something to optimize.

ONE-OFF OR ONGOING

A project service has a defined finish. A photographer completes a shoot. An editor completes a manuscript. A contractor completes a repair.

An ongoing service repeats. A bookkeeper closes the books each month. A cleaner returns every week. A virtual assistant performs recurring tasks.

Neither is inherently better. Ongoing work can create more predictable customer relationships, while projects can create clearer endpoints and more flexibility.

CUSTOM OR STANDARDIZED

A highly custom service changes substantially for each customer. A standardized or productized service defines what is included, what the process looks like, and what the customer receives.

Standardization can make a service easier to explain and deliver, but forcing every service into a rigid package can also remove the flexibility customers actually need.

LOCAL OR REMOTE

Some services require physical presence. Others can be delivered entirely online. Some combine the two.

Do not choose remote merely because the overall goal is to make money "online." If your strongest realistic opportunity is a local service that customers discover or book online, it still belongs in the business options worth considering.

INDIVIDUAL OR GROUP

Some expertise can be delivered to several customers at once through workshops, classes, group coaching, or other shared formats. Other services depend on individual attention.

The question underneath all four dimensions is the same: what does one additional customer require from you?

EXAMPLE: ONE SKILL, SEVERAL SERVICE SHAPES

Suppose you are a photographer.

A one-off custom service might be a two-hour family photo session designed around each family's needs.

A more standardized offer might define a 20-minute mini-session, one location, a fixed number of edited images, and a repeatable booking process.

A local service requires you and the customer to be in the same physical place. Remote photo editing could use related skills without requiring that.

An individual lesson gives one student your attention. A small workshop teaches several people during the same block of time.

These choices affect what the work feels like before they affect marketing. A highly custom service may give you creative freedom but require more planning per customer. A standardized service may reduce planning and make capacity easier to understand, but it can fit fewer unusual requests. Group delivery can serve more people at once, but customers receive less individual attention.

Choose the shape you can realistically deliver now. You can redesign it later.

WHAT "PRODUCTIZED SERVICE" MEANS

The phrase sounds like turning a service into a product, but you are still selling a service.

The difference is standardization.

Imagine a designer who normally says, "Tell me what you need and I'll quote a custom project." Every customer can create a different scope, timeline, process, and price.

A productized version might be, "I create a five-page starter website for local service businesses. It includes these five page types, one design direction, two revision rounds, and a defined delivery process for a fixed package price."

The designer still performs work for each customer. But the shape of the work is more repeatable.

That can make workload, pricing, onboarding, and capacity easier to understand. The tradeoff is that customers needing something outside the package may not fit.

Productization is therefore a way to reduce variation in a service, not a magical way to remove the labor.

IF SEVERAL SERVICE SHAPES COULD WORK

Start with the version you could realistically deliver to your first few customers.

You do not need to design the final scaled company before you have delivered the service.

A custom one-off project can later become a standardized package. A local service can add remote elements. Individual delivery can become group delivery where appropriate. A one-off service can become recurring if the customer genuinely has a recurring need.

Choose the first workable delivery structure, then let real experience show you what should change.

THE DECISION

Choose the service shape you could realistically deliver to your first customers. You can change the structure later as real delivery teaches you where customization, capacity, location, or recurring work becomes a constraint.

One service term worth knowing is SCOPE.

Scope means what is included in the service and what is not. If a bookkeeping package includes monthly transaction categorization and reconciliation but not tax preparation, that boundary is part of the scope.

Clear scope protects both sides because the customer knows what they are buying and you know what you are agreeing to deliver.

WHERE TO GO NEXT
Once the service has a likely operating shape, take it to PDF 43 for pressure-testing. If the underlying service idea still feels wrong, return to PDF 40 or 41.
